newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Generali Israel acqusition faces delay.
newsitem.headline: Generali Israel acqusition faces delay.

text.p: Assicuraziono Generali's takeover of an Israeli insurer will be delayed while officials determine whether the Italian firm is liable for life insurance claims by descendants of Holocaust victims, an Israeli lawmaker said on Wednesday.

Michael Kleiner, who heads the Israeli parliament's insurance sub-committee, said he did not expect insurance commissioner Doron Shorer to approve the takeover until the panel meets for a second session on the claims next week.

He said that in the meantime the committee and Shorer would investigate what legal claims could be made against the Italian insurance company over life insurance policies issued to Jews who later died in the Nazi Holocaust.
A spokesman for the Treasury confirmed that Shorer would wait at least a week.
The dispute arose as Generali prepared to make a $300 million tender offer to shareholders in Israel's Leumi Insurance Holdings.

The offer was supposed to have been made last month but has been held up by the need for government approvals, which officials said were not connected with the Holocaust-related claims. The offer would leave Generali with 57 percent of Leumi Insurance, Israel's biggest insurance company.
"We see it as a very serious matter that Generali will not accept any obligation to investigate the matter of compensation," Kleiner said after the insurance committee met.
He said the panel demanded that the Italian insurer make available policies dating from the era and still held by the company that could verify claims.
Sources involved in the matter said they expected Shorer would approve the Generali takeover if the company showed goodwill by promising to investigate claims.

Last week a Generali spokesman in Milan said the company could not be held responsible for claims relating to Eastern European Holocaust victims, saying that claims should be made to the governments of the region.
Kleiner said families might be able to make a legal claim because Generali policies issued in Poland covered damages outside the country.
I. Amihud Ben-Porath, an attorney representing Generali in Israel, said the company had yet to take a position on the question of making ex gratia payments which would assume no legal obligation.
Ben-Porath told Reuters he still expected to win approval from the insurance commissioner shortly.

Earlier in the week, anti-trust authorities cleared the takeover. Ben-Porath denied newspaper reports approval was snagged by Shorer's demanding a veto over future key appointments at Leumi Insurance.
"To the best of my knowledge, this is not an issue," he said.
